<Rep. Jamie Raskin>: The terrorist atrocities committed by Hamas in Israel on October 7th and the subsequent devastating war in the region have been a colossal human catastrophe. We hope in the coming weeks that a ceasefire can be negotiated so that we will see the return of all the hostages to their families and an end to the gruesome violence and suffering.
At markup, we agreed to advance this bill, which passed the House with near-unanimous support last Congress. No one affiliated with Hamas, nor anyone involved in the horrific attacks of October 7th, should be admissible to the United States or eligible for any immigration benefits, whatsoever. That is an obvious political and moral statement.
This is, however, another missed opportunity for us to work across the aisle in a bipartisan manner. As noted at our markup, this is essentially a visa sanctions bill. For decades, we have relied on pre-negotiated, bipartisan, and bicameral text for every visa sanctions bill. H.R. 176 departs from this bipartisan practice by directly amending the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) to impose visa sanctions. To put into perspective just how unusual this approach is, consider our response to the September 11th attacks. In the aftermath of that national tragedy, we revised our immigration laws to overhaul significant parts of our immigration system, and we created the Department of Homeland Security. Yet, even then, we did not amend the INA to specifically reference the events of September 11th, or to bar the individuals involved in the planning or commission of those attacks from entering or remaining in the United States.
The reason for that is plain: the laws we have in place already bar noncitizens who engage in terrorism or are involved with terrorist organizations, from entering the United States. And for any of those noncitizens who happen to be here, our laws allow us to remove them and prevent them from obtaining any immigration benefits. These laws were designed to apply broadly to any individual or organization engaged in terrorism, without having to specify them by reference to specific events and attacks.
Under sections 212(a)(3)(B) and 237(a)(4)(B) of the INA, any noncitizen who has engaged in terrorist activity, provided material support to terrorists, or is a member or representative of a terrorist organization or a group that endorses or espouses terrorist activity, is inadmissible to the United States and deportable. Hamas has been designated as a terrorist organization since 1997. So, we already have the legal tools to keep any noncitizen involved with Hamas, as well as any noncitizen who was involved in the horrific attacks of October 7th out of this country or deport them if they are already here.
The Committee's standard visa sanctions language--which was carefully crafted in collaboration with all four corners of the Judiciary Committees staff--would allow us to achieve the aims of this legislation without departing from negotiated sanctions language and amendingthe INA in an unprecedented and incongruous way. Amending the INA to impose visa sanctions sets a dangerous precedent where new statutory language becomes necessary every time a new terrorist group emerges. This ad hoc pastiche approach will lead to unintended consequences.
Jamie Raskin,
Ranking Member.
